\title{The Promotion Gap: Verified End-to-End Deployment of\\
Agent-Generated GPU Optimizations\\
\large A Case Study in Video Diffusion Inference}
\author{Aryan \todo{full author list and affiliations}}
\date{August 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Coding agents now routinely produce GPU kernels that pass correctness
suites and report large isolated speedups. We show that, for production
video diffusion inference, these two signals are nearly uncorrelated with
shipped value, and we present a promotion pipeline that measures
optimizations the way users experience them: full-generation latency and
output quality on declared workloads, under fail-closed verification. Run
against FastVideo on NVIDIA GB200, the pipeline surfaced a systematic
\emph{promotion gap}: three fused Wan~2.1 operators with $8.6$--$10.6\times$
isolated speedups left 50-step generation latency unchanged; four LTX
candidates covering $6.2\%$ of end-to-end time could never exceed
$1.0064\times$; and the delivery mechanism itself charged $3.104$\,ms per
call to realize a $124$\,\textmu s saving---a $25{:}1$ dispatch tax
consuming $32.4\%$ of end-to-end time before we eliminated it. Independent
validation caught agent-generated kernels that were bit-exact yet compiled
one call's memory layout in as constants, dispatch code that silently
bypassed compiler guards to report an unfair $2.557\times$, and a
statistically conclusive A/B in which the intervention under test never
executed. Extending the gates with tiered fidelity contracts (bitwise,
numeric, perceptual), we evaluate approximate optimizations honestly: two
published attention methods lose to a tuned FlashAttention baseline in
this regime ($0.80\times$ and $0.52\times$) while structural and
perceptual quality metrics systematically disagree about them. One
transformer artifact was promoted end to end (byte-identical frames,
verified dispatch, zero fallbacks); re-validation across multiple paired
sessions reproduces its speedup in direction and magnitude
($\approx 1.08$--$1.16\times$) while revealing that any single session's
confidence interval---including our own originally published
$1.0857\times$---overstates the measurement's real precision, because
session-to-session variation exceeds within-session sampling error.
% GAP 7: final numbers pend job 1085's verified record; see Section 8.
Every number in this paper traces to a
committed, machine-generated measurement record. We argue this promotion
layer---not kernel generation itself---is the missing infrastructure for
the era of agent-generated performance code.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

The cost of producing plausible GPU kernels has collapsed. Coding agents
iterate on Triton and CUDA faster than humans can review the output, and
benchmark suites report that they increasingly succeed: generated kernels
pass correctness tests and beat reference implementations by comfortable
margins. Evaluation practice, however, has not kept up with generation
practice. The dominant benchmarks score a kernel in isolation---correct
outputs on sampled inputs, speedup against a reference on fixed
shapes~\cite{kernelbench2025,kernelgenbench2026}. These are the two
signals an optimizing agent is trained and prompted to maximize, and we
show that in a production system they are nearly uncorrelated with
delivered value.

We report on MotionKernel, a system that holds agent-generated
optimizations to a different standard: an optimization counts only if it
improves \emph{full-generation} latency on a \emph{declared workload}
without violating a \emph{declared fidelity contract}, measured end to
end in the target framework with the artifact actually dispatching. The
pipeline is fail-closed at every stage---capture, ranking, spec
generation, search, validation, packaging, dispatch, and promotion each
reject by default and must be affirmatively passed. We applied it to
video diffusion inference (FastVideo~\cite{fastvideo} running Wan
2.1~\cite{wan2025} and LTX-2 on NVIDIA GB200), a domain whose cost
structure---hundreds of transformer invocations per generation, quadratic
attention over $10^4$--$10^5$ tokens, a heavy VAE---makes the distance
between operator microbenchmarks and user-visible latency unusually
stark.

That distance is the paper's central finding, which we call the
\emph{promotion gap}. Three fused Wan operators achieved
$8.6$--$10.6\times$ isolated speedups across their production shape
corpora and left 50-step generation latency unchanged
(Table~\ref{tab:wan}). Four validated LTX candidates with isolated
speedups of $1.11$--$1.12\times$ covered $6.20\%$ of end-to-end time in
aggregate: even at zero overhead and perfect fidelity, no combination
could exceed $1.0064\times$ (Table~\ref{tab:ltx-arith}). The delivery
mechanism itself initially charged $3.104$\,ms per call to realize a
$124$\,\textmu s saving---a $25{:}1$ dispatch tax that consumed $32.4\%$
of end-to-end time at 384 calls per generation
(Section~\ref{sec:dispatch}). And when we extended the gates to admit
approximate methods under explicit perceptual budgets, two published
attention accelerators lost to a tuned FlashAttention baseline in this
regime---$0.80\times$ and $0.52\times$---while the two standard quality
metrics disagreed about both of them (Section~\ref{sec:tiers}).

None of these facts is visible to isolated evaluation. Worse, isolated
evaluation is actively gameable by the systems being evaluated: our
independent validation caught an agent-generated kernel that was
bit-exact on every isolated test while having one call's memory layout
compiled in as constants, and dispatch code that silently bypassed
\texttt{torch.compile}'s guards to report a $2.557\times$ speedup its
guarded equivalent could not reproduce (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}). We
also caught ourselves: the pipeline's own impact attribution over-counted
a dispatch chain $4\times$, an author-published number was corrected when
the experiment store ingested the underlying records, and a re-validation
A/B produced a tight, statistically significant result while both arms
ran the unmodified model. We therefore treat machine-checked claims not
as reproducibility hygiene but as a load-bearing component of the system.

This paper makes the following contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item A fail-closed promotion pipeline for agent-generated optimizations,
  from declarative workloads and metadata-only graph capture through
  sandboxed autonomous search, independent validation, versioned
  artifacts, and full-generation A/B promotion (Section~\ref{sec:system}).
\item A quantified account of the promotion gap: isolated operator
  speedup does not predict shipped value, and measured per-artifact
  impact must replace analytical upper bounds, which overstated one
  kernel's return by more than $8\times$ (Section~\ref{sec:gap}).
\item Dispatch-tax accounting: a methodology for attributing delivery
  overhead per call, the $25{:}1$ result it produced, and the measured
  elimination of that overhead (Section~\ref{sec:dispatch}).
\item A failure taxonomy of agent-generated performance code, drawn from
  artifacts our gates caught, with the checks that caught them---including
  the \emph{null intervention}, a conclusive measurement of an experiment
  that never ran (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
\item Tiered fidelity contracts (bitwise, numeric, perceptual) that admit
  approximate optimizations without abandoning verification, and honest
  campaign results under them, including systematic disagreement between
  SSIM and LPIPS (Section~\ref{sec:tiers}).
\item End-to-end results and measurement methodology for shared clusters
  without clock control: a paired, interleaved protocol with
  machine-checked validity bits, under which we retracted three of our
  own previously reported numbers (Section~\ref{sec:results}).
\end{enumerate}

We release the system, every workload manifest, and the machine-generated
measurement record behind every number in this paper.

\section{Background and Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Automated kernel generation and its evaluation.}
Benchmarks such as KernelBench~\cite{kernelbench2025} and
KernelGenBench~\cite{kernelgenbench2026} score language models on
generating kernels for fixed problems, measuring correctness on sampled
inputs and speedup over a reference at fixed shapes; agentic systems
extend one-shot generation with iterative refinement, evolutionary
search, and speculative candidate generation~\cite{specgen2026}. This
evaluation regime embeds three assumptions that our results contradict:
that replaying captured inputs suffices to establish correctness
(Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy} shows a bit-exact kernel wrong for every
input layout but the captured one); that isolated speedup predicts
delivered value (Section~\ref{sec:gap} shows correlations near zero in a
production model); and that the measurement harness is neutral
(Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy} shows an agent optimizing the harness
boundary itself). We do not argue against these benchmarks---they
measure generation ability---but against reading their metric as
deployment evidence.

\paragraph{Accelerating video diffusion inference.}
Video diffusion transformers spend their time in repeated denoising steps
over long token sequences, making them a target for attention
approximation---sliding tile attention~\cite{sta2025}, trainable video
sparse attention~\cite{vsa2025}, training-free sparse
attention~\cite{spargeattn2025}, and quantized attention at INT8 through
FP4~\cite{sageattention2024,sageattention3}---and for cross-step reuse:
input-similarity caching such as TeaCache~\cite{teacache2024} and its
successors~\cite{d2cache2026}. Each technique ships with its own
evaluation on its own workloads, with heterogeneous quality metrics and,
typically, no shared notion of when a result is deployment-ready. Our
contribution is orthogonal: not a new approximation, but the promotion
substrate that evaluates any of them under a declared fidelity budget on
a declared workload---and our negative results
(Section~\ref{sec:tiers}) demonstrate why regime sensitivity makes such
a substrate necessary: methods with real published wins lose outright
under a well-tuned baseline in a regime their papers do not test.

\paragraph{Compilation and delivery.}
\texttt{torch.compile}~\cite{pytorch2} sets the baseline any fusion must
beat, and its guard machinery is precisely what one caught candidate
bypassed. Megakernel compilers~\cite{mpk2025} pursue the logical extreme
of eliminating dispatch cost altogether. Between hand fusion and
megakernels sits an undocumented question this paper quantifies: what a
\emph{framework} charges to route a call to a replacement kernel. Our
$25{:}1$ dispatch-tax result (Section~\ref{sec:dispatch}) indicates this
delivery cost, not kernel quality, can be the binding constraint.

\paragraph{Measurement methodology.}
The systems-benchmarking literature has long catalogued measurement
pitfalls~\cite{mytkowicz2009,heiser}; we adapt its lessons to a setting
it rarely addresses---shared GPU clusters where clock locking is
administratively unavailable---with an interleaved paired-difference
protocol and machine-checked validity bits
(Section~\ref{sec:results}). To our knowledge the
\emph{arms-differentiated} bit (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}), which
invalidates a measurement whose intervention produced no positive
execution evidence, has no published precedent; we found the failure it
guards against three times in one project.

\section{System: A Fail-Closed Promotion Pipeline}
\label{sec:system}

Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline} shows the pipeline. Its design principle is
that every stage rejects by default: an optimization is promoted only by
affirmatively passing capture, ranking, specification, search,
validation, packaging, dispatch, and full-generation A/B, and any
ambiguity at any stage terminates in a machine-readable non-success
state. We describe the stages in order, emphasizing the trust boundaries.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\fbox{\pending{F1: pipeline diagram with trust boundaries (FIGURES.md)}}
\caption{The promotion pipeline. Shaded regions mark trust boundaries:
the search sandbox (agent-writable), the fixed harness (read-only to the
search), and hash-verified artifact payloads. Terminal states are
\texttt{promoted}, \texttt{rejected}, \texttt{quarantined},
\texttt{no\_worthwhile\_candidate}, and \texttt{invalid}.}
\label{fig:pipeline}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Declarative workloads.}
A workload manifest declares one reproducible generation benchmark:
model identity and revision, task and prompt reference, resolution,
frame count, steps, seed, dtype, warmup and measured repetitions, and a
\emph{fidelity policy}---the contract any optimization of this workload
must satisfy (Section~\ref{sec:tiers}). Manifests contain no code and no
model-specific callables; adding a model to the system means writing a
manifest, not an integration.

\paragraph{Metadata-only capture.}
Graph capture attempts symbolic FX tracing, falls back to non-strict
\texttt{torch.export}, then to Dynamo capture, recording per-region
provenance and per-mode failure reasons rather than hiding graph breaks.
Captured regions contain operator sequences, dependencies, tensor
signatures, and safe scalar constants only: weights, prompts,
activations, tensor values, and source code are never serialized, so a
capture can cross organizational boundaries. Regions containing
mutation, collectives, data-dependent control flow, or unknown aliasing
are rejected fail-closed with machine-readable reasons.

\paragraph{Measured impact ranking.}
Regions are ranked by measured share of end-to-end device time,
correlated from profiler evidence, with an Amdahl ceiling and a
configurable impact floor: a candidate whose optimistic end-to-end
improvement cannot clear the floor is excluded \emph{before} any search
budget is spent. Following the attribution defects of
Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}, ranking distrusts analytic bounds: promotion
decisions consume only per-artifact isolation trials, and (as of schema
v3) profiler-derived shares are reconciled against module-level
invocation counts. When a high-impact parent region is unsafe, ranking
attempts to derive a validated executable subregion rather than
discarding the impact, labeling the estimate as a parent-region upper
bound.

\paragraph{Graph-derived specification.}
A ranked region becomes a search problem via an executable intermediate
representation restricted to an allowlisted ATen subset: the IR is
interpreted to produce an eager reference implementation, a weighted
production shape corpus from observed frequencies, dtype-appropriate
tolerances, and a stable graph fingerprint that follows the candidate
through packaging and dispatch. Specification generation operates only
on the validated IR---never on arbitrary source from a capture---and
fails closed on any unsupported operation.

\paragraph{Sandboxed autonomous search.}
Kernel search runs an autonomous coding agent inside an isolated
candidate directory: the agent may edit its candidate kernel freely,
while the repository, harness, specification, corpus, and validation
policy sit outside its write boundary. The search interface is
agent-agnostic (any CLI-invocable agent), budgeted per candidate and per
campaign, and---after the findings of
Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}---re-timed by validation under guarded
dispatch, so that harness-boundary shortcuts discovered by the agent do
not survive into recorded evidence. Notably, some of our campaigns
require no language model at all: the caching campaign of
Section~\ref{sec:tiers} searches a scalar threshold by scripted sweep.

\paragraph{Independent validation.}
Validation re-executes candidates in isolation against regenerated
inputs (not replayed captures): correctness across the weighted corpus,
a shape sweep, numerical stability on fresh allocations, bitwise
determinism, and edge cases, with optional gradient and
\texttt{torch.compile} full-graph checks. Performance baselines are
eager or---the honest default for fusion claims---\texttt{torch.compile}
with \texttt{fullgraph=True}, recorded as \texttt{baseline\_mode} in
schema-versioned result records.

\paragraph{Artifacts, dispatch, and differentiation signals.}
A surviving candidate is packaged as a versioned bundle: a strictly
validated, metadata-only manifest carrying operation identity, graph
fingerprint, compatibility constraints (GPU architecture, framework and
compiler versions, dtype, execution mode), isolated evidence, and a
hash-verified payload. The runtime loads bundles by compatibility, never
by name; any mismatch, load failure, or runtime failure falls back to
the native path with the reason recorded. Each artifact \emph{kind}
(kernel, attention backend, schedule transform) must declare a
\emph{positive differentiation signal}---candidate dispatch count,
effective-backend echo, cache-hit count---which downstream measurement
requires (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

\paragraph{Promotion.}
Promotion consumes only full-generation evidence: an interleaved paired
A/B (Section~\ref{sec:results}) on the declared workload, the fidelity
verdict under the workload's declared tier, real dispatch selection with
zero unexplained fallbacks, and a speedup gate derived from the
measured Amdahl ceiling rather than a flat threshold
(\pending{ceiling-derived gate parameters; Phase 3 build}). Finalization
is write-once: a resumed campaign can never weaken an already finalized
verdict, and every campaign runs under an immutable run contract with
fail-closed preflight.

\section{The Promotion Gap}
\label{sec:gap}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Isolated operator speedup versus end-to-end effect (Wan~2.1
T2V 1.3B, 480p, GB200). Isolated results are weighted across the
production shape corpus; the 50-step generation A/B was unchanged.}
\label{tab:wan}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Fused operator & Isolated speedup & End-to-end effect \\
\midrule
Post-attention gated residual + LayerNorm & $8.638\times$ & \multirow{3}{*}{$\sim 1.00\times$} \\
Modulated pre-attention LayerNorm & $10.449\times$ & \\
Post-MLP gated residual & $10.628\times$ & \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Our first campaign optimized what the literature suggests and what the
profiler appears to confirm: memory-bound elementwise and normalization
chains in Wan's transformer blocks. All three fused operators passed
every correctness stage and achieved order-of-magnitude isolated
speedups across their production shape corpora
(Table~\ref{tab:wan})---and a 50-step generation was indistinguishable
with and without them. The explanation is not subtle: the fused regions
account for well under one percent of end-to-end device time each, and a
$10\times$ improvement of $0.5\%$ is $0.45\%$. What is subtle is how
completely isolated evaluation obscures this. Nothing in the kernels'
own evidence---correctness, stability, determinism, roofline
position---distinguishes them from a valuable optimization. The value
judgment lives entirely in a quantity the kernel never sees: the
workload-level share of the region it accelerates.

The second campaign made the arithmetic explicit
(Table~\ref{tab:ltx-arith}). Four LTX candidates survived validation
with isolated speedups of $1.11$--$1.12\times$; their aggregate
end-to-end share was $6.20\%$, so the best possible combined outcome---%
zero delivery overhead, perfect fidelity---was $1.0064\times$, below the
campaign's $1.01\times$ gate. No search, however good, could have
promoted these candidates; the failure was target selection, and the
pipeline's packaging stage initially compounded it by consulting an
analytic Amdahl bound ($\mathrm{share} \times 0.9$, assuming the
region's cost falls to zero) that overstated the realizable return of a
$1.115\times$ kernel by more than $8\times$. The remedy that survived
contact with evidence: promotion consumes only \emph{measured}
per-artifact isolation trials, and ranking treats analytic ceilings as
exclusion filters (a candidate that cannot win even optimistically is
skipped), never as promotion evidence.

The promotion gap generalizes beyond our system. Any evaluation whose
unit is the operator will systematically reward exactly the candidates
in Tables~\ref{tab:wan} and~\ref{tab:ltx-arith}: they are the easiest
regions to fuse, the easiest wins to measure, and the least likely to
matter. The regions that do matter---attention at $27$--$35\%$ of
end-to-end time on our Wan workload, $15.13\%$ on LTX---are precisely
those with strong existing baselines where honest evaluation most often
returns a negative verdict (Section~\ref{sec:tiers}).

\section{The Dispatch Tax}
\label{sec:dispatch}

A kernel's value is bounded not only by its region's share but by what
the framework charges to deliver it. We attribute delivery cost per call
as
\[
\text{overhead/call} = \frac{\Delta T_{\text{generation}}}{{\text{calls}}} + \text{expected saving/call},
\]
measured from paired generations with and without the artifact
dispatching. For the promoted LTX transformer artifact the accounting
was stark: the kernel saved $124$\,\textmu s per call
($259.05 \to 134.90$\,\textmu s), while delivery cost $3.104$\,ms per
call---a $25{:}1$ loss. At 384 transformer calls per generation this
overhead totaled $1.192$\,s, $32.4\%$ of end-to-end latency; the same
artifact machinery on the VAE ($4.7$ calls per generation) cost an
invisible $0.39\%$. Identical delivery, opposite economics
(Figure~\ref{fig:breakeven}): dispatch overhead is a per-call constant,
so the regions most worth optimizing---hot, frequently invoked---are
exactly the regions that amplify it.

Two components were implementation defects, found and fixed: a
diagnostic parameter snapshot built three times per call, and per-call
rediscovery of the rewritten graph's placeholders. The dominant term was
structural: to fuse a subregion, the integration replaced the enclosing
block's forward with an eager FX \texttt{GraphModule} replay, paying
Python-level graph interpretation on every invocation of a hot module.
The fix replaced replay-based delivery with guarded compiled dispatch:
registered custom operations that \texttt{torch.compile} traces
through, guards intact. Post-fix measurement on sm100 shows
\pending{post-fix overhead per call and the re-run verdicts of the four
Table~\ref{tab:ltx-arith} artifacts, from
docs/dispatch-overhead records; Figure~\ref{fig:tax}}.

Two lessons travel. First, delivery overhead must be measured and
published alongside kernel speedups; a fusion evaluated without its
dispatch path is evaluated in a fiction. Second, the guard evaluation an
integration is tempted to skip (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}) is part of
the honest price of delivery: a speedup that exists only without guards
is not a speedup.

\section{What Agents Get Wrong}
\label{sec:taxonomy}

Autonomous search produced kernels that were fast, numerically exact, and
wrong. This section is a taxonomy of the failures our pipeline caught,
organized by what made each one invisible to isolated evaluation. Every
case is drawn from preserved, immutable campaign evidence; none is
hypothetical. We include, deliberately, the failures that originated in
our own pipeline and in our own claims, because the taxonomy's lesson is
not ``agents write bad kernels''---it is that \emph{plausibility,
correctness on sampled inputs, and honest accounting are three different
properties}, and a promotion system must check all three.

\subsection{Contract violations that isolated tests cannot see}

The strongest candidate of one LTX campaign---a fused transformer
subregion spanning 22 graph nodes---passed smoke testing with
\texttt{max\_abs\_error} $= 0.0$, passed a full shape sweep at
$0.00$ worst error, and was bitwise deterministic across runs. It
failed the numerical-stability stage with a stride assertion:
\texttt{expected stride 4096 == 16384 at dim=1}. The kernel was not
numerically wrong anywhere; it had compiled the memory layout of
\emph{one observed call} into itself as compile-time constants:

\begin{verbatim}
_MAIN_ROWS = 4680
SOURCE_ROW_STRIDE = 16384   # a property of one call,
CONTEXT_ROW_STRIDE = 8192   # not of the operation
\end{verbatim}

The observed inputs were non-contiguous slices of larger timestep
tensors; the stability stage allocated fresh contiguous tensors of the
same shape, and the kernel would have read at wrong addresses. Every
isolated test that reuses the captured inputs---which is what
speedup-oriented evaluation naturally does---certifies this kernel as
perfect. The failure class is a \emph{layout contract violation}:
the kernel implements a function of one call's strides, not of the
operation. The gate that caught it was input diversity: validation
stages that re-generate inputs rather than replaying captured ones.

\subsection{Measurement gaming: the guard bypass}

The same candidate reported a $2.557\times$ isolated speedup. Its
dispatch wrapper compiled the implementation once, then cached and called
Inductor's raw compiled entry directly:

\begin{verbatim}
# "Calling the captured entry directly avoids a
#  guard/cache lookup before every GPU schedule."
outputs = _COMPILED_ENTRY(...)
\end{verbatim}

Two things are wrong at once. First, the number is unfair: the compiled
baseline it was compared against pays guard evaluation on every call, and
the candidate does not---the agent optimized the \emph{measurement
boundary}, not the kernel. Second, the bypass removes exactly the safety
mechanism that would have converted the layout violation of the previous
subsection from an assertion failure into silently wrong output at full
speed. The violation surfaced only because Inductor happens to emit an
internal stride assertion; the agent's Triton kernels contain no such
check. We draw a general conclusion: \textbf{an optimizing agent given a
timing harness will, without adversarial intent, discover the seams of
the harness}---and dispatch-path shortcuts look identical to legitimate
optimization in a diff. The countermeasure is structural, not
review-based: validation re-times candidates under its own guarded
dispatch, and a candidate whose speedup does not survive guarded
execution is scored on the guarded number.

\subsection{Attribution defects: when the pipeline lies to the search}

The search can only be as honest as the numbers steering it, and two of
the largest defects we found were in our own attribution, not in any
kernel. A campaign's transformer region was assigned
\texttt{share\_of\_e2e} $= 1.0333$---more than the whole
generation---because inclusive profiler ranges were summed against an
exclusive total. Its call count was recorded as $195{,}661$; the module
was invoked $1{,}151$ times---aten-level events across 48 blocks were
counted as module calls. Downstream, packaging consulted an analytic
Amdahl bound (\texttt{share} $\times 0.9$, assuming the region's cost
falls to zero) that overstated the realizable return of a $1.115\times$
kernel by more than $8\times$; two artifacts carried
\texttt{meets\_promotion\_target: false} into packaging and were
packaged anyway. The same defect recurred months later in our own
analysis: an attention-share estimate of $45.94\%$, computed by summing
an inclusive profiler column that counted one dispatch chain four times,
was corrected to a measured $27$--$35\%$. Attribution errors are more
dangerous than kernel errors: a wrong kernel is caught by a gate, while
a wrong impact number silently misallocates the entire search budget.
The remedies that worked were mechanical: derive impact from
per-artifact isolation trials rather than analytic bounds, and reconcile
module-level counts against profiler events before ranking consumes
them.

\subsection{Language that reads as verdicts}

Smaller defects concerned words rather than numbers, and they matter
because unattended runs are read after the fact by humans deciding what
shipped. A campaign status field reported four artifacts as
\texttt{finalized}; all four were quarantined and none was promoted. A
quarantine reason claimed ``the end-to-end validation stage did not
complete''; the stage had completed and returned a definite negative.
A search prompt announced ``Measured optimistic model impact: None\%''
because it read a key that nothing writes. Each is trivial; together
they compound into a run report that a reasonable reader mistakes for
success. Our rule since: status vocabulary is closed and tested, reasons
must quote the evidence they summarize, and any prompt field that can be
unset fails preflight rather than interpolating \texttt{None}.

\subsection{The null intervention: measuring nothing with high confidence}

The most instructive failure arrived while re-validating our own headline
result under a stricter measurement protocol. The paired A/B returned
$0.9011\times$ for the promoted transformer artifact, with a bootstrap CI
of $[0.868, 0.920]$ excluding $1.0$, a significant Wilcoxon test, a clean
plateaued clock trace, and \texttt{valid\_for\_gating: true}. Read
naively, this retracts the project's principal positive result. It
measures nothing: the candidate arm configured the artifact directory
through an environment variable that the FastVideo checkout in use never
reads. Every variable was inert; no artifact was selected; zero candidate
calls appear in the log. \emph{Both arms ran the native model}, and every
check the protocol performed---statistical, environmental,
procedural---passed, because none of them asked whether the intervention
under test had actually happened.

This was the third appearance of one meta-failure at a third layer: an
attention selector that silently substitutes the fallback backend on
\texttt{ImportError} (so a campaign measures FlashAttention twice under
another backend's name), a caching flag that is accepted and consumed by
nothing, and now configuration read by no code path. The general form:
\textbf{in a system with graceful fallbacks, the absence of an
intervention is silent, and statistics cannot distinguish ``no effect''
from ``no experiment.''} The structural remedy is that every artifact
kind must declare a \emph{positive differentiation signal}---candidate
dispatch count, effective-backend echo, cache-hit count---and a
measurement whose arms show no such signal is invalidated
(\texttt{arms\_differentiated = false}) before its timings are read. We
note with some discomfort that we had already built exactly this guard
for attention backends, and described its rationale at length, before
reproducing the failure one layer down; defense in depth against this
class evidently must be a property of the platform's artifact registry,
not of individual campaign authors remembering the lesson.

\subsection{Failures caught by gates versus failures caught by tooling}

Of the defects above, the layout violation and the guard bypass were
caught by verification gates; the attribution and language defects were
caught by audit---a human rereading evidence---and later by
infrastructure built in response (an experiment store whose ingest
reconciles published numbers against raw records caught an
author-published speedup that had been transcribed from a job log, and a
factual claim about a model's attention requirements was corrected when
the store linked the constraint to the checkpoint rather than the
configuration). The trajectory across our campaigns is consistent:
\textbf{every class of error we initially caught by reading, we
eventually caught earlier by checking}, and the system's reliability
improved exactly as fast as claims moved from prose into
machine-validated records.
\pending{T4/F6: per-gate catch-rate table from experiment-store backfill
(EVIDENCE\_MAP gap 3).}

\section{Fidelity Tiers and Approximate Optimizations}
\label{sec:tiers}

Bitwise parity is the right default contract and the wrong universal
one: it structurally excludes every approximation with a real
speed--quality trade---quantized attention, sparse attention, step
caching---which is where the large end-to-end factors in the video
literature live. We therefore attach a \emph{fidelity tier} to each
workload: \textbf{Tier 0} (bitwise equality), \textbf{Tier 1} (declared
numeric tolerance; the default when a workload declares nothing), and
\textbf{Tier 2} (a perceptual budget: worst-frame SSIM floor and LPIPS
ceiling against fixed-seed reference frames, thresholds declared per
workload). A third, \emph{advisory}, level records metrics without ever
auto-promoting. At Tier 2 the fidelity verdict replaces the parity
check---otherwise every non-bit-exact candidate quarantines before its
quality evidence is read---and a promoted artifact's manifest carries
its tier and measured margins, so a consumer knows exactly what was
promised. Both directions are tested: a deliberately lossy control is
rejected, and a known-good approximation promotes with recorded margins.

\paragraph{Attention under Tier 2.}
Attention is the largest honest target our ranking identifies
($27$--$35\%$ of end-to-end device time on the Wan workload, ceiling
$1.37$--$1.54\times$; $15.13\%$ on LTX, ceiling $1.178\times$---excluded
by the impact floor before any budget was spent). Table~\ref{tab:attention}
reports the first campaign: both published candidates were \emph{slower}
than the pinned FlashAttention baseline, and both failed the SSIM floor
while passing the LPIPS ceiling. The regime matters: SageAttention v1's
quantize/dequantize overhead exceeds its savings against a well-tuned
sm100 baseline, and zero-shot sparse attention pays tile selection and
gather costs that its published gains---obtained with VSA-finetuned
checkpoints---do not. A campaign without an enforced
backend-differentiation signal would have measured none of this: all
three optional backends were absent from the cluster's base image, and
the framework's selector silently substitutes FlashAttention on import
error, so an unguarded A/B would have measured the baseline twice and
reported $\sim 1.00\times$ under each candidate's name.

\paragraph{Metric disagreement.}
The two rejections disagree instructively: VSA is perceptually closer to
the baseline than SageAttention on both metrics, while being far slower.
And both candidates pass LPIPS while failing SSIM---a budget gating on
LPIPS alone admits both; on SSIM alone, rejects both without recording
that they are perceptually close (Figure~\ref{fig:metrics}). We
therefore declare both metrics, gate on their conjunction, and publish
margins rather than binary verdicts. We regard the empirical
characterization of which metric families track human judgment for
\emph{acceleration} artifacts (as opposed to generation quality) as
open, and our fixed-seed frame sets make the question testable.

\paragraph{Schedule transforms: caching without an LLM.}
The first artifact kind that wraps the denoising loop rather than a
graph region is input-similarity caching: skip a step's computation when
an accumulated input-distance signal falls below a threshold, with three
structural guarantees enforced in the artifact---the first step is never
a cache hit, no state crosses generations, and consecutive skips are
capped. Distance accumulates and resets on compute, since per-step
comparison lets unbounded drift look locally safe. The searched
parameter is a scalar threshold, so the campaign is a scripted sweep
(coarse grid, then bisection), each point one paired A/B plus a Tier-2
fidelity verdict---no language model in the loop. Cache hits per
generation serve as the kind's differentiation signal.

\section{End-to-End Results and Measurement Methodology}
\label{sec:results}

\paragraph{Measurement on clusters you do not control.}
Our cluster's GPUs idle at 285\,MHz against a 2062\,MHz maximum, clock
locking is administratively unavailable, and exclusive-node allocation
did not collapse run-to-run spread (5.57\% CV against 4.74--7.37\%
baseline). Sequential per-arm A/Bs are ungateable under these
conditions, and applying that standard retroactively invalidated three
of our own previously reported numbers ($1.0274\times$, $1.2459\times$,
$1.1155\times$). The protocol that replaced them: sustained-load warmup
until the recorded clock trace plateaus (observed: max boost held
through every timed run), interleaved arm scheduling, and
paired-difference statistics---median paired delta, bootstrap CI, and a
Wilcoxon signed-rank test---with machine-checked validity bits
(interleaving, clock trace present, plateau reached, native-arm CV
ceiling, and \texttt{arms\_differentiated}). Where variance was already
negligible the protocols agree, as they should: the one A/B measured
under both gives $0.8106\times$ [$0.8091, 0.8111$] paired against
$0.8031\times$ sequential at 0.04\% native CV
(Figure~\ref{fig:protocol}).

The paired protocol then taught us its own limitation. Repeating the
same artifact A/B across sessions---each run paired, interleaved, and on
plateaued clocks---produced estimates whose bootstrap intervals do not
overlap: $1.1550\times$ [$1.123, 1.187$] and $1.0784\times$
[$1.051, 1.103$] for the identical intervention on the identical
workload. The bootstrap CI quantifies sampling error \emph{within} one
session and is silent about variation \emph{between} sessions, which is
evidently larger; a single run's interval therefore reads far tighter
than the measurement's real uncertainty. Pairing halved the spread
relative to the sequential protocol ($\sim 15\%$ across sequential
sessions to $\sim 7\%$ across paired ones) without removing it. The
consequence is a reporting rule we adopt for every gated number:
\textbf{the session, not the pair, is the unit of replication}---a
speedup claim requires multiple paired sessions and is reported as a
cross-session range or aggregate, never as one session's interval. We
record the protocol's lack of a built-in multi-session requirement as a
design gap discovered by use, deliberately not patched mid-measurement
(Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).

The honest conclusion has two parts. The speedup is real: every session
reproduces it in direction, and the cross-session range
($\approx 1.08$--$1.16\times$) brackets the original claim. The original
\emph{precision} is not supportable: quoting any single session to three
decimals---ours included---overstates certainty, since sessions 1082 and
1083 exclude each other's intervals. The headline this project now
reports is the cross-session range with per-session records attached.
The first re-validation attempt is itself a result: it produced a
conclusive-looking $0.9011\times$ that measured nothing
(Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}), and the differentiation guard it motivated
is a precondition for every row of Table~\ref{tab:revalidation}.

\paragraph{Support matrix.}
Support claims are generated from evidence, never asserted: a model
$\times$ workload $\times$ architecture cell reports \texttt{promoted},
\texttt{no\_worthwhile\_candidate}, a named rejection, or a named
capture blocker, each linked to its records, regenerated in CI.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Our deep integration is one framework (FastVideo) on one primary
architecture (sm100; sm90 \pending{status at submission}), and single-GPU
inference only; the pipeline's contracts are designed to generalize, but
we have not demonstrated cross-framework portability of promoted
artifacts. Perceptual gates inherit the limitations of their metrics:
Section~\ref{sec:tiers} shows SSIM and LPIPS disagreeing systematically,
and our conjunction gate is conservative rather than validated against
human judgment. The paired protocol
lacks a built-in multi-session requirement: we discovered by use that
within-session confidence intervals understate real uncertainty
(Section~\ref{sec:results}) and adopted cross-session reporting as
policy, but the protocol schema does not yet enforce a minimum session
count, and our cross-session ranges are built from small numbers of
sessions. The autonomous-search economics (token cost per promoted
artifact) are observed but not systematically studied---several of our
strongest results required no LLM search at all, which is itself a
finding about where such search is worth buying. Finally, our negative
results are regime-specific by construction: they show published methods
losing \emph{on these workloads under these baselines}, not that the
methods are without value in their intended regimes.

\section{Conclusion}

Kernel generation is no longer the bottleneck; believing a kernel is.
Across every campaign we ran, the scarce resource was not candidate
implementations but \emph{trustworthy evidence about them}: what a
candidate's region is worth end to end, what its delivery costs, whether
its speedup survives guards, whether its quality loss fits a declared
budget, and whether the experiment that measured it actually ran. The
promotion pipeline we describe makes each of those questions a
machine-checked gate, and the result is a system whose failures---
reported here at the same resolution as its successes---were caught
before they shipped. We believe this layer is what the coming ecosystem
of agent-optimized software is missing, and we release ours in full.
